polio-vaccine.summary: Paralytic polio became a recurring terror of twentieth-century summers until the 1955 vaccine; the disease is now close to eradication.
polio-vaccine.significance: Paralytic polio was a recurring terror of twentieth-century summers; it is now endemic in two countries.
polio-vaccine.note: From the epidemic era through the 1955 vaccine to the launch of the global eradication initiative.

heisenberg.summary: Formulated the first complete quantum mechanics and the uncertainty principle, which sets a hard limit on what can be known at once.

dirac.summary: Merged quantum mechanics with special relativity and, from the equation's spare solutions, predicted antimatter.

von-neumann.summary: Whose report on the EDVAC described storing a program in the same memory as its data — the architecture nearly every computer since has used, and the reason software can be written rather than wired.

herero-nama-genocide.summary: German colonial forces in South West Africa drove the Herero into the desert and interned survivors in camps, killing an estimated 80% of the Herero and half the Nama. Germany formally acknowledged it as genocide in 2021.

oppenheimer.summary: Ran the laboratory that built the first nuclear weapons, argued afterwards against building the far larger one, and had his security clearance taken away for it.

panama-canal.summary: Cut the sea route between the Atlantic and Pacific by thousands of kilometres, after a French attempt had failed and tens of thousands of workers had died, mostly of malaria and yellow fever.

maji-maji-rebellion.summary: A broad uprising against German rule and forced cotton cultivation in East Africa, suppressed by a scorched-earth campaign that caused famine killing perhaps a quarter of a million people.

sartre.summary: Held that we exist first and define ourselves afterwards, so freedom is inescapable and responsibility total.

hannah-arendt.summary: Analysed totalitarianism as a new form of rule and argued that great evil is often done by unremarkable people who stop thinking.

hopper.summary: Wrote the first compiler and argued that programs could be written in something closer to English, which became COBOL and with it most of the world's business software.

frida-kahlo.summary: Painted mostly herself, from a bed and a body wrecked by a streetcar at eighteen, in a Mexican visual language she chose deliberately over the European one — and was known in her lifetime largely as Diego Rivera's wife.

de-beauvoir.summary: Argued that woman has been constructed as the other against which man defines himself, founding modern feminist philosophy.

mexican-revolution.summary: A decade of civil war against a thirty-year dictatorship, which produced land reform, a constitution that was radical for its time, and something close to a million deaths.

stolen-generations.summary: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were removed from their families by state policy for six decades. The 1997 Bringing Them Home report documented the consequences; a national apology followed in 2008.

xinhai-revolution.summary: Ended two thousand years of imperial rule and founded a republic that promptly fragmented among warlords.

turing.summary: Defined what a computing machine is and what it can never decide, broke wartime ciphers, and was prosecuted for being gay.
turing.significance: He defined what a computer is before any existed, and what no computer can ever decide. The device you are reading this on is an instance of his abstraction.

first-world-war.summary: Industrial production turned on an entire continent's young men for four years, killed some seventeen million people, brought down four empires, and settled little enough that the next war is often read as its second half.

irish-independence.summary: The Easter Rising, war, and then a treaty that partitioned the island — a sequence of rising, repression and partition that recurred across the British empire.

shannon.summary: Showed in a master's thesis that Boolean algebra describes switching circuits, then founded information theory — the bit, channel capacity, and the proof that reliable communication over a noisy line is possible at all.

russian-revolution.summary: Two revolutions in one year removed the Tsar and then the provisional government, and a civil war left the Bolsheviks holding the first state founded on Marx — which the rest of the century organised itself around, for and against.

feynman.summary: Built a working quantum theory of light and matter and a diagram notation that made its calculations tractable.

influenza-1918.summary: Infected roughly a third of humanity and killed more people than the war that spread it, with unusually high mortality among healthy young adults.
influenza-1918.note: Estimates range from 17 million to 50 million deaths and occasionally higher; India alone may account for a fifth. Wartime censorship means the contemporary record is poor.

image.credit: Otis Historical Archives, National Museum of Health and Medicine

mandela.summary: Imprisoned for twenty-seven years for his part in the armed struggle against apartheid, he negotiated its dismantling on release and became the first president elected by all South Africans.

ravi-shankar.summary: Took the sitar and the Hindustani raga to concert halls that had no idea what to do with them, taught George Harrison, and spent the rest of his life insisting the music was older and stranger than the audience thought.

rosalind-franklin.summary: Produced the X-ray diffraction images that revealed DNA's helical structure, used to reach that conclusion without her knowledge.

soviet-central-asia.summary: Moscow drew five republics along ethnic lines that had not existed as political borders before, forcibly settled nomads at enormous cost in life, and turned much of the region over to cotton.

image.credit: Cacahuate, Russian translation by Peter Fitzgerald

hilbert-program.summary: The question of whether a mechanical procedure could decide any mathematical statement. Answering it no forced Church and Turing to define what a mechanical procedure is, which is where the computer comes from.

mlk.summary: Led the American civil rights movement on a strategy of disciplined non-violence taken in part from Gandhi, won the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts, and was assassinated at thirty-nine while supporting a strike by sanitation workers.

dijkstra.summary: Gave the shortest-path algorithm every routing system uses, and spent the rest of his life insisting that programming is a mathematical discipline and that most of the industry was doing it wrong.

second-sino-japanese-war.summary: Japan's invasion of China, which merged into the Second World War and cost more Chinese lives than any other conflict of the century.
second-sino-japanese-war.note: Chinese casualty estimates run to 20 million, most of them civilians. Japanese and Chinese accounts of specific atrocities, notably at Nanjing, remain a live diplomatic dispute.

image.credit: Unknown photographer, Ministry of the Navy

second-world-war.summary: The deadliest conflict in history, ending with the first use of nuclear weapons and a settlement that divided the world into two camps for the next forty-five years.
second-world-war.note: The start depends where you stand. 1939 is the invasion of Poland; 1937 is the full Japanese invasion of China, which is where the fighting began for the theatre that lost the most people.

knuth.summary: Who set out to write one book on compilers, is still writing The Art of Computer Programming sixty years later, and wrote a typesetting system from scratch because the proofs looked wrong.

image.credit: Flickr user Jacob Appelbaum, uploaded to en.wikipedia by users BeSherman, Duozmo

holocaust.summary: The murder of about six million Jews, alongside Roma, disabled people, Poles, Soviet prisoners and others, by the German state and its collaborators — organised bureaucratically, with records, by an industrialised country in the middle of Europe.
holocaust.note: The bracket covers the systematic extermination; the persecution began with the 1933 boycotts and the 1935 Nuremberg laws, and the entry does not pretend that 1941 is where it started.

eniac.summary: Eighteen thousand valves filling a room, programmed by rewiring it, and operated largely by women mathematicians whose work went uncredited for decades.
eniac.note: Which machine was first depends on the definition. Colossus ran at Bletchley Park in 1943 but was secret until the 1970s and not general-purpose; the Z3 was programmable but electromechanical. ENIAC was electronic, general-purpose, and public.

bob-marley.summary: Carried reggae out of Kingston and made a small island's music a global language of resistance — and, two days after being shot, played the concert anyway.

image.credit: Dennis Morris; Distributed by Island Records

cold-war.summary: Two nuclear-armed blocs that never fought each other directly and fought almost everywhere else through proxies — ending when one of them dissolved rather than when either won a battle.

image.credit: U.S. Army photo Photo Credit: USAMHI

hiroshima-nagasaki.summary: The only use of nuclear weapons in war, killing well over a hundred thousand people, most of them instantly, and ending the Second World War days later.

indonesia-independence.summary: Declared days after the Japanese surrender, then defended through four years of war before the Netherlands conceded.

vietnam-independence.summary: Declared in 1945 and secured against France at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, which partitioned the country and set up the war that followed.

pacific-nuclear-testing.summary: The United States, Britain and France conducted over three hundred nuclear tests across the Pacific, displacing populations from Bikini, Enewetak and Moruroa, several of whom have never been able to return.

image.credit: Jack W. Aeby, July 16, 1945, Civilian worker at Los Alamos laboratory, working under the aegis of the Manhattan Project.

indian-independence.summary: British India was partitioned into the dominions of India and Pakistan, ending colonial rule and displacing some fifteen million people.
indian-independence.significance: The largest and fastest mass migration in history, with a border drawn in five weeks by a lawyer who had never been to India. Its consequences are still being fought over.

south-asia-partition-wave.summary: India and Pakistan in August 1947, Burma and Ceylon the following year — the first and largest wave of post-war decolonisation, and the template for what followed in Africa.

transistor.summary: Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley at Bell Labs replaced the valve with a sliver of semiconductor — the component that made computers small, cheap and cool enough to be everywhere.

apartheid.summary: A legal system classifying every person by race and allocating where they could live, work, study and whom they could marry accordingly. It stripped Black South Africans — the large majority — of citizenship, assigning them to nominally independent homelands.
apartheid.significance: Its end in 1994 is within living memory for most adults. On this timeline it sits closer to the present than the Moon landing does.

sources.title: South African History Online — Apartheid legislation

israel-founded.summary: The British mandate ended and Israel declared independence, immediately followed by war with neighbouring Arab states.
israel-founded.note: The same events are known to Palestinians as the Nakba, in which roughly 700,000 people were displaced. Both descriptions refer to the same year and are recorded here without adjudication.

prc-founded.summary: The Communist victory in the civil war ended four decades of warlordism, invasion and revolution.

korean-war.summary: Ended in armistice rather than peace, leaving a division that has now lasted longer than the unified state that preceded it.

image.credit: All photographs are works of the United States federal government.

african-independence-wave.summary: Within three decades almost every African colony became independent, inheriting borders drawn in Berlin, economies built for extraction, and in several cases immediate civil war.

arab-independence-wave.summary: Libya in 1951, Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia in 1956, Kuwait 1961, Algeria 1962 after a brutal eight-year war, and the Gulf states by 1971.

dna-structure.summary: The double helix explained at a stroke how heredity is stored and copied.
dna-structure.significance: The structure explained the function immediately - a molecule shaped to be copied. Few discoveries answer their own question so completely.

algerian-war.summary: Eight years of war, torture and mass displacement ended 132 years of French rule and brought down the French Fourth Republic.
algerian-war.note: Death tolls are heavily disputed — French estimates around 350,000, Algerian accounts closer to 1.5 million.

ghana-independence.summary: The first sub-Saharan colony to gain independence, under Kwame Nkrumah, whose pan-Africanism set the terms for the wave that followed.

great-leap-forward.summary: A forced collectivisation and industrialisation drive that produced the deadliest famine in recorded history.
great-leap-forward.note: Excess-death estimates range from 15 to 55 million, with 30 million often cited. The Chinese state has never published a full accounting.

integrated-circuit.summary: Kilby and Noyce independently put a whole circuit on one piece of semiconductor, which is what made it possible to keep doubling the number of components on a chip for the next fifty years.

aral-sea.summary: Soviet irrigation diverted the two rivers feeding what was the world's fourth-largest lake; it has lost most of its volume, leaving a salt desert, a collapsed fishery and a public health crisis.

image.credit: NASA, derivative work by Zafiroblue05 at en.wikipedia

beatles.summary: Eight years in which popular music went from two-minute singles to the album as a form — and in which the recording studio became an instrument rather than a room for capturing a performance.

sharpeville-massacre.summary: Police fired on a crowd protesting the pass laws, killing 69 people, most shot in the back. It ended the era of non-violent protest, drove the liberation movements underground, and turned world opinion.

year-of-africa.summary: Seventeen African countries became independent in a single year, including Nigeria, the Congo, Senegal, Madagascar and Somalia. The continent's political map changed more in twelve months than in the previous sixty years.

image.credit: Original uploader was Mehmetaergun; recreated by Nobelium (talk) 2010-05-10

east-africa-independence.summary: Tanganyika in 1961, Uganda 1962, Kenya 1963 after the Mau Mau insurgency and its suppression, Zambia and Malawi 1964.

samoa-independence.summary: The first Pacific Island nation to gain independence in the twentieth century, opening a wave that ran through Fiji and Tonga in 1970.

cultural-revolution.summary: A decade of mobilised political violence that closed universities, destroyed historical artefacts and monasteries, and displaced or killed intellectuals, officials and teachers in enormous numbers.

smallpox-eradication.summary: A coordinated global vaccination campaign eliminated smallpox entirely — the only human disease ever deliberately driven to extinction, after it had killed an estimated 300 million people in the twentieth century alone.

image.credit: Content Providers(s): CDC/ Dr. Fred Murphy; Sylvia Whitfield

arpanet.summary: Packet switching between four American universities, grown into a protocol that assumes the network is unreliable and lets any network join.
arpanet.note: The bracket runs from the first ARPANET link to the switch to TCP/IP, which is the date the internet as a network of networks begins rather than any single machine connecting.

moon-landing.summary: The first crewed landing on another world.

bangladesh-independence.summary: East Pakistan broke away after a war marked by mass killing and the displacement of ten million refugees into India, which intervened decisively.
bangladesh-independence.note: Bangladeshi accounts give three million killed; independent estimates range from 300,000 upward. The scale is disputed, the atrocity is not.

lusophone-independence.summary: Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde became independent after a coup in Lisbon ended the dictatorship that had fought to keep them; Angola and Mozambique slid straight into long civil wars.

png-independence.summary: Independence from Australian administration, for a country holding over eight hundred languages — more linguistic diversity than any other state on Earth.

soweto-uprising.summary: School students protesting compulsory instruction in Afrikaans were shot at by police; the images that followed made apartheid internationally indefensible and triggered a decade of sustained revolt.

reform-and-opening.summary: Market reforms under Deng Xiaoping moved several hundred million people out of poverty within a generation, the fastest such change ever recorded.

zimbabwe-independence.summary: Majority rule after fifteen years of unilateral white minority government and a guerrilla war to end it.

hiv-aids.summary: Identified in 1981 and traced to a mid-century crossover from primates in central Africa. It has killed over 40 million people; the antiretroviral therapies developed from 1996 turned it from a death sentence into a manageable condition for those who can obtain them.

world-wide-web.summary: Tim Berners-Lee's proposal at CERN for linking documents across the internet, released without patent or licence fee — the decision that let it become the default way people use a computer.

human-genome.summary: Sequenced the three billion letters of human DNA and published the result openly.

namibia-independence.summary: The last African colony to become independent, having passed from German to South African rule and been held in defiance of the UN for decades.

pacific-sea-level.summary: Low-lying atoll states including Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Marshall Islands face the loss of habitable land within this century, having contributed almost nothing to the emissions causing it.

soviet-dissolution.summary: Fifteen republics became independent states in a single year, including the Baltic states, Ukraine and the Central Asian republics — the last great wave of new countries.

mabo-decision.summary: Australia's High Court rejected the doctrine that the continent had belonged to no one before 1788, recognising for the first time in law that Indigenous people held title to their land.

south-africa-1994.summary: All South Africans voted together for the first time, ending apartheid. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission that followed chose public testimony over prosecution, a bargain still argued about.
